title: How disrupted spatial fluxes reshape food web structure along the river–sea continuum
text:
Anthropic disturbances and ecosystem processes transcend the artificial boundaries between land, freshwater, and sea. While these systems are interconnected through species and material fluxes, they are often studied in isolation. In response, the concept of metaecosystem has emerged as a powerful framework to understand how fluxes among ecosystems shape their functions and dynamics. Disrupting these fluxes can have dramatic consequences that ripple across entire landscapes. In aquatic systems, dams and nutrient pollution are known to strongly affect fish communities. Yet, little is still known about how these effects propagate and potentially accumulate, through hydrographic basins and ultimately to the sea. Using bayesian spatio-temporal statistical models (R-INLA), we aim to analyse existing data on food-web structure across France, combined with environmental variables (dams, nutrients, …), to quantify how breaking or increasing fluxes among systems disturbs food-web structure locally and how these disturbances spread throughout the metaecosystem.
Keywords: foodweb ecology, stream network, spatial autocorrelation, bayesian statistics.

title: How disrupted spatial fluxes reshape food web structure along the river–sea continuum
text:
Introduction
While patterns in community change within river network have been well studied, these studies have mostly focus on specise richness (Bonnaffé et al. 2024a), or roughly defined functional composition (Vannote et al. 1980).

Barnes et al. (2026) food web complexity mediates diversity-functioning relationship. Interesting metric of trophic complementarity, could be used for our study if we can formulate clear hypothesis of stressors on that metric.
Lindgren and Rue (2015) R-INLA paper


River-estuary-sea continuum

Xenopoulos et al. (2017) highlights the importance of accounting for the full gradient from headwater to the sea. Freshwater and coastal ecosystems are connected by flux of carbone and nutrients (N, P), as well as, movement of migratory species. Reviews work connecting river and sea, that said, most of them focus on chemical fluxes, remain relatively local, and none of them focused on the food web structure.
Catchment land-use impacts macro-invertebrates along the river-sea continuum with no dilution effect (Bierschenk et al. 2017).
The Land-to-Ocean Continuum (LOAC) concept has been used to study carbon fluxes between land and ocean, and how these fluxes, and feedback loop influence the carbon storage by oceans (Regnier et al. 2022).
Hong et al. (2015) Editorial overview of studies investigating the impact of human pressure along the river-estuary-sea continuum, more focused toward biochemistry than ecology.
Ouellet et al. (2022) provides a conceptual model (DWOC) to advance a more holistic management of diadromous species across the watersheds-ocean continuum.
Tee et al. (2021) studies the river-to-sea continuum of microbial communities through community composition and their function (nutrient cycling).
Whitfield et al. (2024) reviews how species richness changes along the salinity gradient in estuaries. As we go to freshwater to brackish water we loose species richness, and as we to brackish water to the sea we recover species richness.
Elliott and Quintino (2007) argues that it is difficult to detect the effect of anthropogenic pressure in estuary as estuaries are already stressed environment. In particular, this means thinking about the indicators used to describe ecosystem states (diversity, and functionning).
Little et al. (2017) Lechêne et al. (2018) Olli et al. (2019) and Freitas and Araújo (2025) study how communities change along environmental gradient in estuaries.
Attrill (2002) critiques Remane diagram and proposes and quantitive, testable alternative that consider salinity ranges instead of salinity.
Macedo et al. (2021) Food webs are simpler during the dry season than the rainy season in the estuarine and neritic zones. During the rainy season, the food web of the neritic is largely shaped by migratory species from the estuarine and oceanic areas.
Álvarez-Romero et al. (2015) proposes an integrated framework to include land-use change in cactchement in the impact on coastal biodiversity.
Truchy et al. (2026) links metaecosystem and ecosystem services theories to develop an unified framework for managing sociohydroecosystems.
Potter et al. (2015) review and categorize the different ways fish use estuaries.



Freshwater ecosystems

The River Continuum Concept has shaped the freshwater ecology researsh by links physical gradients along rivers to predictable changes in community structure, energy sources, and ecosystem functioning (Vannote et al. 1980; Doretto et al. 2020).
Serial Discontinuity Concept is a framework to predict the impact of discontinuities, such as dams, on biotic and abiotic variables along the river continuum (Ward and Stanford 1995).
The Flood Pulse Concept (FPC) complements the RCC as it focuses on the lateral dimension of rivers and its role in explaining community productivity, while the RCC focused on the longitudinal aspect. The FPC states that its the rythm of flood and recession – that is, the pulse – which structures ecosystem productivity, not the flow (Junk et al. 1989).

Terrestrial organic matter (leaf litter, vegetation, soil nutrients) gets dissolved and mobilized into the water
Aquatic plants and algae explode in productivity in the shallow, sunlit floodwaters
Fish and invertebrates move onto the floodplain to feed and reproduce
When waters recede, nutrients and organic matter flush back into the main channel

The River Wave concept as unifying framework of different concepts of freshwater ecology (Humphries et al. 2014).
Community richness and hence food web structure is expected to be driven by nutrient availability (Ho et al. 2023).
Carraro and Ho (2025) link river shapes community diversity and food web structure using a numerical approach. Higher spatial heterogeneity and lower biomass in elongated rivers than compact ones, driven by higher variability in nutrient input load.
Harris et al. (2026) mobile consumers (fish, birds) use heterogeneous resources in braided river, New Zealand.
Garcia et al. (2025) invasive make trophic structure more stable in lake fish communities (France)



Multiple stressors

Synergistic and antagonistic effects of multiple stressors (Jackson et al. 2021; Orr et al. 2024).
Temperature can interact with nutrients and impact food web structure in a nonlinear way Binzer et al. (2012).
(Danet et al. 2021; Bonnaffé et al. 2024a).
Zhang et al. (2026) precipitation modulates human impacts on riverine food webs



Connectivity

Small dispersal stabilizes through spatial structure and asynchrony (LeCraw et al. 2014; McCann et al. 2005; Pillai et al. 2011).
A metaecosystem model shows that dispersal of living organisms (that consume nutrients) is stabilising,while dispersal of non-living compartments such as nutrients or detritus is destabilising (Gounand et al. 2014).
Prey switching of mobile top predators can stabilize connected food webs through ‘spatial coupling’ (LeCraw et al. 2014; McCann et al. 2005; Pillai et al. 2011).
At high dispersal/connectivity the stabilizing effect wanes as strongly connected patches behave as a single patch (LeCraw et al. 2014; McCann et al. 2005).
Studies between pairs of the following connectivity, complexity and stability are common. However, studies investigating how these are interconnected are rare (LeCraw et al. 2014).
Connectivity has 4 dimensions: longitudinal, lateral, vertical and temporal (Grill et al. 2019).
We identified five pressure factors to represent the main human interferences within the four dimensions of fluvial or river connectivity (Grill et al. 2019):

river fragmentation (longitudinal);
flow regulation (lateral and temporal);
sediment trapping (longitudinal, lateral and vertical);
water consumption (lateral, vertical and temporal);
infrastructure development in riparian areas and floodplains (lateral and longitudinal).

In freshwater system, fish dispersal is limited. A meta-analysis found that the mean dispersal kernel is around 10km (Comte and Olden 2018).
Neutral metacommunity model explains biodiversity pattern in the Mississipi river, showing the key role of dispersal in explaining community structure along the river continuum (Muneepeerakul et al. 2008).
Connectivity structures and mititgates effect of drying events in macroinvertebrates communities (Chalmandrier et al. 2025).
It is key to adopt a network perspective to understand how diversity is created and maintained within riverine ecosystems (Altermatt 2013). With this perspective one can account for the dendritic network and so the spatial processes that shape diversity.
From points (Death and Winterbourn 1995)… to lines (RCC, SDC)… to dendritic networks (Shepherd and Ellis 1997).
River network characteristics, local network properties and their interaction were important individual contributors to explaining local species richness of aquatic insects (Altermatt et al. 2013). Effect of connectivity on richness supported experimentally (Carrara et al. 2012).
Altermatt and Fronhofer (2018) in exprimental microcosms population densities are found to be more heterogeneous in dendritic than linear networks.
Campbell Grant et al. (2007) the geometry of dendritic network interacts with species movement and reshape population densities and interaction network.



Decomposing spatio-temporal patterns

Frelat et al. (2022) decompose change in food web structure and species composition across space and time using a tensor decomposition. We could probably try the method for our work.
Kortsch et al. (2021) investigates change in food web in the Baltic Sea using weighted and unweighted structural metrics.



Dams

Decrease river connectivity / reduce migration (Dean et al. 2023; He et al. 2024; Pedersen et al. 2012).
Reservoir, lotic from lentic conditions, can result in hypoxic conditions. Favor phytoplancktons and macrophytes (Ding et al. 2026; Dean et al. 2023). Facilitate the spread of invasive species (Johnson et al. 2008).
Reservoir increase residence time of nutrients upstream and decrease the downstream output, which can result in a decrease in primary productivity.
Hydropeaking - that is, the sudden release of large water to answer the higher electric demand - can harm riverine community due to sudden change in water level and water flow.
Cumulative impact of dams can reduce the nutrient input in deltas (Dean et al. 2023).
A review (Ellis and Jones 2013) suggests that two recovery gradients exist in regulated river:

a longer, thermal gradient of around 100 km;
a shorter resource subsidy gradient of around 1-4 km.

Zhu et al. (2024) shows that dam areas show lowest richness and highest connectance, while areas with dam removed show highest richness but lowest connectance.
Dolan et al. (2026) Meta-analysis shows that native and non-native species increased after barrier removal, but the positive effect was strongest for native species
Chan et al. (2025) dam have negative impact on diadromous fish species. The installation of fish passes didn’t have a positive effect. Dam removal had a positive effect.
Van Looy et al. (2014) Dam impacts on fish communities is dominated by local rather regional effects in the Loire basin.



Nutrients

Mwanake et al. (2026) DOC-to-nutrient ratios in river decline worldwide
Ma et al. (2026) finds that human impact destabilize riverine fish communities, but habitat complexity buffers this destabilizing effect.



Meta-ecosystems

Loreau et al. (2003) fundational paper that defines the concept of meta-ecosystem.
Polis et al. (1997) founding synthesis of how spatial subsidy, flux of consumer and resources reorganise food webs.
Nakano and Murakami (2001) shows the seasonal coupling between a forest and stream, where subidies flux alternate between season. Flux from aquatic to terrestrial peaked in spring, while the reciprocal flux peaked in summer.
Leibold et al. (2004) provides a definition for the concept of meta-community and present different paradigms: patch dynamic, species sorting, mass effect and neutral perspective. See also Loreau et al. (2004).
Duffy et al. (2007) reviews of study incorporating trophic complexity in BEF literature.
Spaak et al. (2026) provide a metric of coupling between ecosystems based on the Jacobian.
Peller et al. (2026) Nested flows of nutrients and consumers stabilize metaecosystems through cross-scale source-sink dynamics.
Govaert et al. (2026) disturbance responses can be modified by local resource availability and cross-ecosystem flows.



Traits






Note



This section may not be relevant for the current manuscript. It may however be useful resource for future extension of the project that may include trait space analysis.



Brosse et al. (2021) FISHMORPH database which contains 10 morphological traits for around 50% of freshwater fish species worldwide.
Su et al. (2023) in North American freshwater, invasive species are often highly fecund, long-lived and large. Invaded community on the other hand exhibit a high functional distance between the species it comprises leaving empty functional space for potential invaders.
Toussaint et al. (2018) Non-native species led to marked shifts in functional diversity of the world freshwater fish faunas

title: How disrupted spatial fluxes reshape food web structure along the river–sea continuum
text:
Hypotheses
Building on the causal structure below (Fig. 1) and the literature reviewed above, we formulate four hypotheses.

We focus on three structural metrics with well-developed theoretical expectations: connectance, mean trophic level, and a trophic complementarity metric following Barnes et al. (2026). Because connectance, and potentially other structural metric, are mechanically linked to species richness (Cohen and Briand 1984; Martinez 1992) we will incorporate richness as mediator variable to separate direct and richness-mediated effects .

H1: Nutrients have a unimodal effect on food web structure
We expect an overall humped relationship between nutrient availability (proxy of productivity) and food web structure (Mittelbach et al. 2001). Moderate nutrient enrichment should increase local productivity and prey availability, supporting more diverse and complex food webs (Ho et al. 2023; but see Post 2002). Beyond a threshold, excess nutrients are expected to degrade food web structure through hypoxia, algal dominance, and turbidity (Ding et al. 2026; Dean et al. 2023), or through the destabilization of higher trophic level as predicted by the paradox of enrichment (Rosenzweig 1971). This is consistent with Bonnaffé et al. (2024b)’s recent finding that temperature and nutrient interact magnifying food web simplification. In sum, we expect mean trophic level and trophic complementarity to rise then fall with nutrient concentration, and connectance to follow the opposite pattern (mostly through richness-mediated effect).


H2: Dams fragment the lanscape but homogeneize biotic community
We distinguish a local pathway (distance to nearest dam) from a global pathway (cumulative barrier effect / basin-wide fragmentation). At the (global) basin scale, cumulative (linear) downstream fragmentation is expected to reduce species richness, mean trophic level and trophic complementarity, through loss of migratory and piscivorous species that depend on longitudinal connectivity (Dean et al. 2023; He et al. 2024). On the other hand, the upstream cumultative fragmentation homogeneize hydrological conditions resulting in more similar biotic community (Poff et al. 2007). As a result, cumulative (dendritic) upstream fragmentation is expected to reduce trophic complementarity and increase connectance through the promotion of generalist – sometimes invasive – species (Johnson et al. 2008; Encina et al. 2024; Bylak et al. 2023). At a local scale, this phenomenon is expected to increase near reservoir and so should be come stronger as the distance to the nearest downstream dam decreases. Conversely, we expect the opposite effect of the distance to the nearest upstream dam because of the negative effect of sediment starvation and hydropeaking on productivity (Ellis and Jones 2013).


H3: The effect of dams and nutrients on food web structure is partly mediated by species richness
Dams and nutrients can impact species richness (as described above), which in turn impacts food web structure. This is an indirect pathway through which stressors can reshape food web. In addition, we predict candidate direct-effect mechanisms to operate. In particular, the impact of invasive species (described in H2) operates both indirectly and directly on food web structure. Indirectly through the potential exclusion of native species, directly through its unique generalist diet. We note, as a limitation, that the mediated effect from richness to food web structure may also capture the impact of other confounding factors acting on species richness and food web structure independently of stressors (such as habitat complexity).


H4: Stressor impacts change along the river-estuary-sea continuum, and peak in estuaries
We predict that stressor impacts (nutrient and dams) on food web structure — i.e. an interaction between continuum position and stressor magnitude — is not uniform along the continuum. Specifically, because estuaries are naturally stressful environments (fluctuating salinity, turbidity, low baseline diversity), resident communities may already sit closer to their tolerance limits and hence be more sensitive to added anthropogenic pressure (Elliott and Quintino 2007).


H5: Nutrient impact on food web structure is magnified in lentic, dam-impounded reaches
We predict a true stressor-by-stressor interaction: the effect of nutrient concentration on food web structure (H1) is amplified in sites closer to downstream dam because of longer residence time. Impoundment slows water transit, giving phytoplankton more time to take up available nutrients and convert them into biomass rather than being flushed downstream (Chen et al. 2020). We therefore expect the nutrient effect on species richness, connectance, mean trophic level and trophic complementarity to strengthen as distance to the nearest downstream dam decreases, i.e. a nutrient × local-downstream-dam interaction. This tests for a synergestic interaction between nutrient and dam impacts (Jackson et al. 2021; Orr et al. 2024).

title: How disrupted spatial fluxes reshape food web structure along the river–sea continuum
text:
Statistical model
We formalise H1–H5 as two linked Bayesian spatial models fit in INLA, following the mediation structure introduced in H3. Structural metrics (connectance, mean trophic level, trophic complementarity) are fit as separate response models sharing the same covariate structure. Site-level covariates are: nutrient (nutrient concentration or composite index, H1); dam_down_local and dam_down_global (distance to nearest downstream dam, and cumulative downstream fragmentation, H2); dam_up_local and dam_up_global (distance to nearest upstream dam, and cumulative upstream fragmentation, H2); richness (local species richness, H3); and habitat (categorical variable distinguishing river, estuary and sea sites). S(site) denotes the spatial random effect.






Note



S(site) can be a Whittle–Matérn field on the river metric graph (Bolin et al. 2023) for river sites, and a standard 2D SPDE field for coastal sites (if needed, maybe a metric graph will be sufficient if sites are close enough to the river mouth).








Note



We use a categorical variable to caracterise site position along the continuum to avoid identifiability issue. As a continuous variable (e.g. distance to river mouth) may already be captured by the spatial random effect, making the model unable to disentangle the two.


structure ~ nutrient + nutrient^2 # H1
            + dam_down_local + dam_down_global # H2
            + dam_up_local + dam_up_global # H2
            + nutrient:dam_down_local # H5
            + habitat:nutrient # H4
            + habitat:dam # H4
            + richness # H3
            + S(site) # Handle spatial auto-correlation

# H3 - Model richness as a mediator variable
richness ~ nutrient + nutrient^2
           + dam_down_local + dam_down_global
           + dam_up_local + dam_up_global
           + nutrient:dam_down_local
           + habitat:nutrient
           + habitat:dam
           + S(site)






Note



The structure and richness equations above are not a single joint model. Instead, we fit the two models separately. For H3’s mediated pathway, we draw matched posterior samples of the relevant stressor coefficient from the richness fit and the richness coefficient from the structure fit, and multiply them to obtain a posterior distribution for the indirect effect. The direct effect is read directly from the structure model’s stressor coefficient, and the total effect is the sum of the two. This approach is common practice in Bayesian mediation, but it is important to note that it does not fully propagate joint uncertainty.

title: How disrupted spatial fluxes reshape food web structure along the river–sea continuum
text:
Methods

Food web inference
To infer local food web structure, we used a metaweb approach. That is, we build a web compiling the potential feeding interactions between all species of the dataset. Importantly, our metaweb takes into account intra-specific variation in species diet. We did so by defining trophic interactions at different life stages for each species.

Metaweb nodes
The nodes of our metaweb represent a species at a given lifestage. Specifically, fish species were divided into nine body class sizes evenly distributed. Each body size class within a given species is what we call a ‘trophic species’ assuming that conspecifics of the same body size class share similar trophic interactions because trophic interactions are largely determined by predator–prey body size ratio in freshwater ecosystems (Brose et al. 2006).
In addition of fish species, seven basal nodes (resources) were added at the base of the metaweb: detritus, biofilm, phytoplanckton, zooplanckton, macrophytes and zoobenthos. We represent the basal food web structure in the Appendix.  We assumed that these resources were present at all sampling sites.


Infer missing fish lengths
Most length of fishes are measured but not all. Yet, we need individual fish length to determine their diet based on their ontogeny. We infer missing fish size using information on the given fishing operation. When there are more than three observations of the fish species, we use a truncated normal distribution (package truncdist; Nadarajah and Kotz (2006)). The mean and variance are given by the modes of the observed distribution of the fishing operation. The minimum and maximum of the distribution are given by the minimal and maximal length observed on the entire data set for that species. We do so to avoid infering irrealistic lengths.


Get fish diet
We use fishbase as a primary source to extract fish diet at their different life stages, to get on which basal categories species feed on and whether they are piscivorous or not. We detail in the Supporting Information how made the correspondance between our categories and the one of fishbase. We remove species that have an occurence lower than 10 in the entire dataset which comprise 69 species. This enable to avoid retrieving diet information of species that will have a minimal impact on food web structure due to their rarity. We add a larvae stage when missing, assuming that fish larvae feed on zooplankton (Dabrowski 1984). We assume that fish individuals are larvae if they measure less than 2 cm. To classify individuals as juvenile or adult we use the length at maturity of the species as a threshold. When this information was not available we used a single stage (combined) by merging the diets of the two stages. We did not consider a recruit stage.


The metaweb
Predation window are assumed to be 0.03 to 0.45 of individual body size for piscivorous species. We then use the package foodwebbuilder to build the metaweb and the local food webs through subsampling. We investigated the effect of the number of size classes on the structure of the reconstructed metaweb. We observed little influence of the number of size classes on the metaweb connectance Figure S1. So, we decided to split each species 5 size classes as in Bonnaffé et al. (2024a).






Note



The choice of a constant predation window has an important implication. It implies that what only matters in terms of ecosystem functioning is the individual size (once the species is known to be piscivorous). In this setting, two piscivorous individual of different species but same size will eat the very same things.




Subsampling the metaweb to get local food webs

Discussion

Limitations
Regarding food web structure, we have simplified the base of the web and exclude macro-invertebrates. This choice naturally emphasizes the functional role of fishes in shaping food web structures. Yet, it would be valuable to include macro-invertebrates within the food web to get a more exhaustive picture of how aquatic community respond to stressors along the riversea continuum.

The interaction can be synergistic or antagonistic (Orr et al. 2024)
Temperature \(\times\) nutrients

Expected in theory to be antagonistic (Binzer et al. 2012)
But not supported by empirical data (Bonnaffé et al. 2024)

Dam \(\times\) nutrients

Decrease in connectivity which favor accumulation and so eutrophication (Maavara et al. 2020)

Dam \(\times\) dam

Dam have cumulative impact on migratory species (Dean et al. 2023)

title: RIVERSEA Project
text:
In brief

Dams have been reported to have an impact on riverine ecosystem
But studies are mostly local and focused on species richness
Furthermore the interaction of dams with other stressors has not been clearly assessed
Lastly, dam impact could spread to the sea but this propagation has not been investigated

Separation between freshwater and marine ecology
Different survey and dataset
Different interests, terminology, etc.

We aim to link these fields, to answer the following question…

title: RIVERSEA Project
text:
What we have













River and coast/estuary data (respectively provided by Alain and Anik)
Long time series (e.g. Nurse survey started in 1980)

Not always continuous (gaps)
Different protocoles

Species abundances
Individual fish size (sometimes missing)

title: RIVERSEA Project
text:
What we plan to add
For each local community:

Distance to the sea/source
Dams location
Salinity
Temperature
Nutrient concentration
… (any suggestion?)







Caution


Data should be available at each site (or can be infered) along the river-sea continuum.

title: RIVERSEA Project
text:
Measuring the impact of dams

Distance to the closest dam
Height/reservoir volume of the closest dam
Accumulated heights of upstream/downstream dams (Dean et al. 2023)
At what scale dam impacts operate?

Use the literature, but difficult because of varied impacts on species
Make the statistical model infer the scale
\(\text{Dam}_\text{down}(L) = \sum_{i \in \text{dam}} h_i e^{-\frac{d_i}{L}}\)
\(L\) define the scale at which dam operates
Try different values and compare WAIC (that is, model performance)

Quantify structure with connectance and trophic length (a metric weighted by biomass?)

Methods of Bonnaffé et al. (2021).

What we want
How dams reshape food web along the river-sea continuum by disrupting spatial fluxes?

Quantify the impact of dams on food web structure
In space and time
Along the river-sea continuum
Quantify interaction of dam with other stressors
Bonus (liste au Père Noël):

Use spatial correlation to assess flux between ecosystem (meta-ecosystem view)
Predict the impact of dam removal (may be possible with bayesian model)
Sélune project: tracking the impact of dam removal in Britany

title: RIVERSEA Project
text:
The statistical model
Equation
\[
\begin{align}
\text{TL}_i &= \text{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma_i) \\
\text{logit} (\mu_i) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 \text{Dam} + ... ~ \text{[fixed effects]} \\
&+ \text{interactions} \\
&+ \text{random effects}
\end{align}
\]

Account for survey random effects
Account for spatial and temporal auto-correlation
Use a spatiotemporal model (R-INLA)
Possible limitations

Can we distengle survey bias from environment effect?
Until where the concept of continuum holds?
Do we have high variability in dams density between hydrographic bassin?

text:
Roadmap

Build food webs in the coast/estuary
Update food webs in rivers
Collect and infer if necessary environmental data
First perform “coarse-grained” statistical analysis

At the bassin scale: Number of dam vs. Trends [TL vs Distance to the source]
PCA to assess the main environmental drivers of food web structure

Next, refine statistical analysis (R-INLA)…

title: Food web structures along the river-sea continuum
text:
Species composition along the continuum
We start by looking at how much species overlap there is between the three surveys that make up the river-estuary-sea continuum: river (freshwater, ASPE), nurse (estuary and sea) and pomet (estuary and sea).


Code
size <- tar_read(size_year_filtered)
plot_venn_diagram(size)









Three species are shared by all three surveys: Anguilla anguilla (European eel, catadromous), Chelon ramada (grey mullet, euryhaline estuarine migrant) and Platichthys flesus (European flounder, catadromous flatfish).
More surprising is the river/pomet overlap (16 species), which excludes nurse entirely. These 16 are all strict freshwater residents (e.g. roach, bream, perch, pikeperch, barbel, chub, three-spined stickleback), not diadromous species. These species most probably come from pomet fishing operation that occurs deep into the estuaries (Girond and Loire).
So river and open sea share species through because of two reasons. First, through diadromous species that live across the whole continuum. Second, through residents caught by pomet operations deep into estuaries.

title: Food web structures along the river-sea continuum
text:
Metaweb
The metaweb represents every possible predator-prey interaction across the whole continuum, aggregated over all size classes so each species appears as a single node. Species are placed vertically by trophic level, from resources (grey, bottom) up to fish (top), colored by whether they prey on other fish at any life stage, and sized by each species’ mean observed body length.


Code
web_list <- tar_read(web_list)
resource_list <- tar_read(resource_list)
diet <- tar_read(diet)
size <- tar_read(size_year_filtered)
plot_metaweb(web_list$metaweb, resource_list, diet, size)









148 fish species and 10 basal resources make up the metaweb, for a total of 8661 possible interactions at the species level.
Here is the interactive version of the static plot above, so we can zoom in and inspect in more details the metaweb.


Code
species_traits <- tar_read(species_traits)
plot_metaweb_interactive(
  web_list$metaweb,
  resource_list,
  diet,
  size,
  species_traits
)

title: Food web structures along the river-sea continuum
text:
Species-level information
Environment (freshwater/marine/both), demersal/pelagic position and diadromous status come from FishBase’s species() table; native status is FishBase’s country() table filtered to France. Two caveats:

Diadromous status (is_diadromous) is TRUE for FishBase migratory categories that cross the fresh/salt water boundary (amphidromous, anadromous, catadromous), FALSE for every other documented category (non-migratory, potamodromous, oceanodromous), and NA only when FishBase leaves the category genuinely blank rather than coding it “non-migratory”. In practice, almost all NA species are strict freshwater residents (roach, bream, perch, etc.), so read NA as “presumed FALSE” rather than a real unknown.
Native status (is_native) is TRUE or FALSE (“invasive”). The three gobies Neogobius melanostomus, Ponticola kessleri and Proterorhinus semilunaris have no France record in FishBase’s country() table, even though they are documented recent invaders in French rivers in the literature, so they are hardcoded to FALSE rather than left NA.



Code
species_summary <- size |>
  group_by(species_valid) |>
  summarise(
    n_individuals = n(),
    n_operations = n_distinct(operation_id),
    mean_length = mean(length, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(species_traits, by = c("species_valid" = "species")) |>
  arrange(desc(n_individuals))




Code
count_bar <- function(data, var, title) {
  data |>
    count(.data[[var]]) |>
    mutate(
      val = forcats::fct_reorder(
        tidyr::replace_na(as.character(.data[[var]]), "NA"), n
      )
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(n, val)) +
    geom_col() +
    labs(x = "Number of species", y = NULL, title = title)
}

patchwork::wrap_plots(
  count_bar(species_summary, "environment", "Environment"),
  count_bar(species_summary, "is_diadromous", "Diadromous"),
  count_bar(species_summary, "is_native", "Native (France)"),
  nrow = 1
)

title: Food web structures along the river-sea continuum
section: Local food webs along the continuum
text:
Local food webs along the continuum
To see how food web structure evolves along the continuum, we pick three individual operations along Gironde: one on the coast (pomet), one within the Gironde estuary itself (nurse), and one upstream on the Dordogne (river).


Code
foodweb_structure <- tar_read(foodweb_structure)
operation_year_filtered <- tar_read(operation_year_filtered)

ops <- c(
  pomet = "61832307", nurse = "2022_1_GIR12_14_S", river = "83544"
)
titles <- c(
  pomet = "Coast",
  nurse = "Estuary",
  river = "River"
)


First, a map showing where each of the three operations sits along the coastline/estuary/river.


Code
continuum_pts <- operation_year_filtered |>
  filter(operation_id %in% ops) |>
  mutate(
    label = titles[names(ops)[match(operation_id, ops)]]
  )

france <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(
  geounit = "france", type = "map_units", scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf"
)
rivers_fr <- rnaturalearth::ne_download(
  scale = 10,
  type = "rivers_lake_centerlines",
  category = "physical",
  returnclass = "sf"
) |>
  sf::st_intersection(france)

e <- 0.4
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = rivers_fr, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = coastline(), linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(
    data = continuum_pts,
    aes(longitude, latitude),
    color = "black",
    size = 3
  ) +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = continuum_pts,
    aes(longitude, latitude, label = label),
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = range(continuum_pts$longitude) + c(-e, e),
    ylim = range(continuum_pts$latitude) + c(-e, e)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )











Code
# Shared size scale across all three panels, so `guides = "collect"` below
# merges them into a single legend instead of one per panel.
size_range <- (size |>
  filter(operation_id %in% ops) |>
  group_by(species_valid) |>
  summarise(v = mean(length, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"))$v |>
  range()

local_web_plots <- lapply(names(ops), function(nm) {
  fw_row <- foodweb_structure |> filter(operation_id == ops[nm])
  web <- fw_row$foodweb[[1]]
  op_size <- size |> filter(operation_id == ops[nm])
  subtitle <- sprintf(
    "Richness %d · Connectance %.2f · Mean TL %.1f",
    round(exp(fw_row$log_species_richness)), fw_row$connectance,
    fw_row$trophic_length
  )
  plot_local_foodweb(
    web, resource_list, diet, op_size,
    title = titles[nm], size_limits = size_range
  ) +
    labs(subtitle = subtitle) +
    theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, color = "grey40"))
})

patchwork::wrap_plots(local_web_plots, nrow = 1) +
  patchwork::plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









The three webs illustrate a clear shift in composition: the coastal web is built around marine flatfish and with several piscivorous predators; the estuarine web is sparser, dominated by basal resources with only a couple of connected fish; and the river web is dominated by small non-piscivorous cyprinids alongside a handful of large piscivorous predators.

title: Food web structures along the river-sea continuum
text:
Structure metrics along the continuum
Rather than comparing surveys as discrete boxplots, we map each operation’s structure metrics at its actual location, restricted to the Gironde estuary/coast and the Dordogne river, to see how food web structure changes continuously along the gradient instead of as three discrete groups.
We look at trophic length, diet overlap, connectance and species richness. Diet overlap is the mean pairwise Jaccard similarity between predators’ prey sets (low = predators partition prey between them/complementarity, high = predators eat largely the same things/redundancy) - unlike connectance, it is close to independent of species richness (0.28 here vs. -0.54 for connectance), so it adds information richness alone doesn’t already give us.


Code
continuum_box <- foodweb_structure |>
  filter(longitude > -1.8, longitude < 1.3, latitude > 44.3, latitude < 46.0)

plot_metric_map <- function(data, metric, title) {
  ggplot(data) +
    geom_sf(
      data = rivers_fr, color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.3, inherit.aes = FALSE
    ) +
    geom_sf(data = coastline(), linewidth = 0.3, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    geom_point(
      aes(longitude, latitude, color = .data[[metric]]), size = 1.8, alpha = 0.8
    ) +
    coord_sf(xlim = c(-1.8, 1.3), ylim = c(44.3, 46.0)) +
    scale_color_viridis_c() +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL, color = NULL) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
      panel.grid = element_blank()
    )
}




Code
plot_metric_map(continuum_box, "trophic_length", "Trophic length")











Code
plot_metric_map(continuum_box, "diet_overlap", "Diet overlap")











Code
plot_metric_map(continuum_box, "connectance", "Connectance")











Code
plot_metric_map(continuum_box, "log_species_richness", "Log species richness")

title: Food web structures along the river-sea continuum
Interpolation of REPHY data
text: The goal is to interpolate REPHY data – nutrient and oxygen concentrations – when and where fishing operation occured. It means interpolate the variables of interest in space and time. We intend to do so using the Bayesian framework INLA.

title: Interpolation of REPHY data

Todo

title: Interpolation of REPHY data
text:
Setup


Code
library(renv)
renv::load()

Code
library(targets)
library(here)
tar_config_set(
  store = here::here("_targets")

title: Interpolation of REPHY data
text:
Presentation of the data
Here is the REPHY data that we have collected and cleaned.


Code
rephy_data <- tar_read(rephy_data_surface)
str(rephy_data)


tibble [71,984 × 12] (S3: tbl_df/tbl/data.frame)
 $ site_id        : num [1:71984] 1e+06 1e+06 1e+06 1e+06 1e+06 ...
 $ site_label     : chr [1:71984] "Strouanne" "Strouanne" "Strouanne" "Strouanne" ...
 $ sample_id      : num [1:71984] 50157 50157 50158 50158 50159 ...
 $ date           : Date[1:71984], format: "1989-02-09" "1989-02-09" ...
 $ depth          : num [1:71984] 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 ...
 $ depth_unit     : chr [1:71984] "m" "m" "m" "m" ...
 $ longitude      : num [1:71984] 1.68 1.68 1.68 1.68 1.68 ...
 $ latitude       : num [1:71984] 50.9 50.9 50.9 50.9 50.9 ...
 $ parameter_code : chr [1:71984] "NH4" "OXYGENE" "NH4" "OXYGENE" ...
 $ parameter_label: chr [1:71984] "Ammonium" "Oxygène dissous" "Ammonium" "Oxygène dissous" ...
 $ value          : num [1:71984] 0.15 9.23 0.15 7.39 0.15 ...
 $ unit           : chr [1:71984] "µmol.l-1" "mg.l-1" "µmol.l-1" "mg.l-1" ...


For more information see Overview of REPHY data. And, here is the fishing operation data.


Code
foodwebs <- tar_read(local_foodwebs)


Before interpolating anything, we start with a simple picture of where and when the two datasets overlap: REPHY nutrient and oxygen stations on one side, fishing operations from the food web data on the other.

Spatial coverage


Code
sites <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  rephy_data |>
    dplyr::distinct(longitude, latitude) |>
    dplyr::mutate(source = "REPHY station"),
  foodwebs |>
    dplyr::distinct(longitude, latitude) |>
    dplyr::mutate(source = "Fishing operation")
)

ggplot(sites, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = source)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_sf(data = coastline(), inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +
  coord_sf(xlim = range(sites$longitude), ylim = range(sites$latitude)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, color = NULL)









Fishing operations are much more numerous and spatially diffuse than REPHY stations, which are fixed monitoring points. Interpolation will need to be based on REPHY stations that are reasonably close to fishing operations.


Temporal coverage


Code
yearly_counts <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  rephy_data |>
    dplyr::mutate(year = lubridate::year(date)) |>
    dplyr::count(year, name = "n") |>
    dplyr::mutate(source = "REPHY station"),
  foodwebs |>
    dplyr::count(year, name = "n") |>
    dplyr::mutate(source = "Fishing operation")
)

ggplot(yearly_counts, aes(x = year, y = n, fill = source)) +
  geom_col(position = "identity") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_pretty()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of observations", fill = NULL)









Both datasets have good overlap from 2000 onwarrds, which is where we should expect the interpolation to be best supported.

title: Interpolation of REPHY data
text:
Interpolation model
Each REPHY parameter is interpolated with an additive spatio-temporal model, fit with INLA: a spatial Matérn field (via the SPDE approximation), a smooth year trend, and a cyclic month effect to capture seasonality. Values are modelled on the log scale, since concentrations are strictly positive and right-skewed.
\[
\log(\text{nutrient}) = \text{SPDE}_\text{2D} + \text{year}_\text{RW}
                       + \text{month}_\text{RW}
\]
We restrict the data to 2000 onward.


Code
rephy_filtered <- tar_read(rephy_data_sample)



Spatial mesh
We build a mesh, shared across parameters, from all filtered REPHY stations. Its boundary follows the coastline (a non-convex hull) rather than the convex hull of the stations, which would otherwise span the land between the Atlantic and Channel clusters.


Code
mesh <- build_rephy_mesh(rephy_filtered)
plot(mesh, main = "")
points(
  foodwebs$longitude,
  foodwebs$latitude,
  col = "coral",
  pch = 19,
  cex = 0.5
)
points(
  rephy_filtered$longitude,
  rephy_filtered$latitude,
  col = "cyan3",
  pch = 19,
  cex = 0.5
)
legend(
  "bottomright",
  legend = c("REPHY station", "Fishing operation"),
  col = c("coral", "cyan3"),
  pch = 19,
  bty = "n"
)











Cross-validation


Code
n_fold <- 5


We evaluate the model on each of the four parameters with leave-station-out k-fold cross-validation. Stations are split into 5 groups, and each group is predicted from a model trained on the other stations only. This tests spatial generalization and doesn’t let a station’s other-year data leak into the test fold.
We compare our model performence (RMSE, MAE and correlation) against a naive baseline prediction: the training fold’s mean.


Code
set.seed(1)
cv_all <- purrr::map_dfr(unique(rephy_filtered$parameter_code), \(parameter) {
  d_param <- rephy_filtered |> dplyr::filter(parameter_code == parameter)
  cv <- cv_rephy_spde(d_param, mesh, k = n_fold)
  cv$parameter_code <- parameter
  cv
})

cv_all |>
  dplyr::group_by(parameter_code) |>
  dplyr::group_modify(\(cv, ...) {
    metrics <- rephy_cv_metrics(cv)
    baseline <- rephy_cv_metrics(cv, pred_col = "pred_baseline")
    data.frame(
      model = c("SPDE", "Naive baseline"),
      rmse = c(metrics$rmse, baseline$rmse),
      mae = c(metrics$mae, baseline$mae),
      cor = c(metrics$cor, baseline$cor)
    )
  }) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

Across parameters, the SPDE model has lower log-scale RMSE than the naive baseline and correlates positively with observed values, where the baseline is essentially uncorrelated by construction. The spatio-temporal structure is clearly adding information, even if there’s room to improve.


Code
cv_all <- cv_all |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    highlight = dplyr::case_when(
      parameter_code == "PO4" & site_id == 22044027 & year %in% 2011:2013 ~
        "Pont St Maurice (2011-2013)",
      parameter_code == "OXYGENE" & value < 2 * 1.42903 ~ "Hypoxia (< 2 ml/L)",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

ggplot(cv_all, aes(x = value, y = pred, color = highlight)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Other" = "grey40",
      "Pont St Maurice (2011-2013)" = "#d95f02",
      "Hypoxia (< 2 ml/L)" = "#7570b3"
    )
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter_code, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Observed", y = "Predicted (held-out station)", color = NULL)









The highlighted points, on the PO4 panel, show an anomaly at the station Pont St Maurice, that cannot be predicted by its nearest neighbour. This shows that this point cannot be predicted by a smooth model as they are very localized in space and time. Excluding these, we see that the predictions of our model are quite reasonnable.
On the OXYGENE panel, the highlighted points are hypoxia events (< 2 ml/L, i.e. < 2.86 mg/L Diaz and Rosenberg (2008)) unpredictable from neighbouring stations when the station itself is held out.
We will use yearly averages rather than raw values in the next modelling steps, we also plot the same predictions averaged per year (observed and predicted).


Code
cv_yearly <- cv_all |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    value = mean(value),
    pred = mean(pred),
    .by = c(parameter_code, site_id, site_label, year)
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    highlight = dplyr::case_when(
      parameter_code == "PO4" & site_id == 22044027 & year %in% 2011:2013 ~
        "Pont St Maurice (2011-2013)",
      parameter_code == "OXYGENE" & value < 2 * 1.42903 ~ "Hypoxia (< 2 ml/L)",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

ggplot(cv_yearly, aes(x = value, y = pred, color = highlight)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Other" = "grey40",
      "Pont St Maurice (2011-2013)" = "#d95f02",
      "Hypoxia (< 2 ml/L)" = "#7570b3"
    )
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter_code, scales = "free") +
  labs(
    x = "Observed (yearly mean)", 
    y = "Predicted (yearly mean, held-out station)", 
    color = NULL
  )









We see that mechanically averaging per year remove most of the noise. On yearly average our model performs more than fine so we will use this interpolation model to get environmental values at our fishing operations. But before doing so, we will check the structure of the model residuals.


Residual structure

Temporal structure
We check whether the CV residuals still carry spatial or temporal structure.


Code
cv_resid <- cv_all |>
  dplyr::filter(value > 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(resid = log(pred) - log(value))

year_resid <- cv_resid |> dplyr::summarise(resid = mean(resid), .by = c(parameter_code, year))
month_resid <- cv_resid |> dplyr::summarise(resid = mean(resid), .by = c(parameter_code, month))

ggplot(year_resid, aes(x = year, y = resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~parameter_code, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean log-residual")









Code
ggplot(month_resid, aes(x = month, y = resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter_code, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Mean log-residual")









All four parameters show a large residual change in 2000-2003 that then flattens out. it looks like a coverage artifact of the year random walk rather than a missed trend. Month residuals are flat everywhere: the cyclic month term captures seasonality well.


Spatial structure


Code
station_resid <- cv_resid |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    resid = mean(resid),
    n = dplyr::n(),
    .by = c(parameter_code, site_id, longitude, latitude)
  )

ggplot(station_resid, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = resid, size = n)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 1) +
  geom_sf(data = coastline(), inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = range(station_resid$longitude), ylim = range(station_resid$latitude)
  ) +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "steelblue",
    mid = "grey90",
    high = "firebrick",
    midpoint = 0
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter_code) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, color = "Mean log-resid", size = "n")









There is no broad geographic gradient, but a set of estuarine stations are consistently under-predicted. This point to an unmodeled driver of local nutrient-loading that could bias our analysis afterwards. For that reason, we should certainly include distance to the river mouth as covariate to better predict nutrient concentrations at those sites.

library(INLA)

data_inla <- data |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter_out(dam_distance_downstream == 0) |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(lubridate::year(date)),
    site_id = as.integer(sandre_code),
    log_dist_dam_up_std = scale(log10(dam_distance_upstream)),
    log_dist_dam_down_std = scale(log10(dam_distance_downstream)),
    barrier_up_std = scale(barrier_upstream),
    barrier_down_std = scale(barrier_downstream),
    log_phosphorus_std = scale(log10(total_phosphorus)),
    elevation_std = scale(elevation)
  ) |>
  select(
    S,
    year,
    site_id,
    log_dist_dam_up_std,
    log_dist_dam_down_std,
    barrier_up_std,
    barrier_down_std,
    log_phosphorus_std,
    elevation_std
  )


m_S <- inla(
  S ~ log_dist_dam_up_std + log_dist_dam_down_std +
    barrier_up_std + barrier_down_std +
    log_phosphorus_std +
    elevation_std +
    f(site_id, model = "iid") +
    f(year, model = "iid"),
  family = "nbinomial",
  data = data_inla
)

extract_fixed <- function(model, model_name) {
  model$summary.fixed |>
    tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    mutate(model = model_name)
}

fixed <- extract_fixed(m_S, "Richness")

title: How community richness changes along the estuary-sea continuum
text:
We want to model how species richness changes from the estuary to the sea. To do so, we will quantify how the species richness changes along the salinity gradient.
- The project is out-of-sync -- use `renv::status()` for details.

title: How community richness changes along the estuary-sea continuum
How community richness changes along the estuary-sea continuum
text:
Modeling alpha-diversity with salinity
Next, we want to model how species richness changes with salinity. To do that properly with to account for spatial autocorrelation.

library(INLA)
library(fmesher)

coords <- cbind(data$longitude, data$latitude)

mesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d_inla(
  loc       = coords,
  max.edge  = c(0.1, 0.5),
  offset    = c(0.1, 0.3),
  cutoff    = 0.05
)
plot(mesh)
points(coords, col = "red", cex = 0.1, pch = 3)








Using a Spatial Gaussian Random Field on our mesh, we can fit a model that accounts for spatial autocorrelation.

spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
  mesh = mesh,
  prior.range = c(0.5, 0.5),
  prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)
)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coords)

stk <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = data$log_species_richness),
  A = list(A, 1),
  effects = list(
    list(spatial.field = 1:spde$n.spde),
    list(
      intercept = rep(1, nrow(data)),
      salinity = data$salinity,
      is_nurse = data$is_nurse,
      year = data$year
    )
  ),
  tag = "obs"
)

m1 <- inla(
  y ~ -1 +
    intercept +
    salinity +
    is_nurse +
    f(year, model = "iid") + f(spatial.field, model = spde),
  data = inla.stack.data(stk),
  control.predictor = list(
    A = inla.stack.A(stk),
    compute = TRUE
  ),
  control.compute = list(
    waic = TRUE,
    config = TRUE
  )
)

summary(m1)

Next, we can investigate our model.

spde.result <- inla.spde2.result(m1, "spatial.field", spde, do.transf = TRUE)

inla.emarginal(function(x) x, spde.result$marginals.range.nominal[[1]])

[1] 0.210475


This captures the caracteristic range of the spatial autocorrelation. It is quite small, meaning that it acts at a small spatial scale, and our data is not too sensitive to this biais. This may be due to the act that our data is quite noisy due to fishing operations that may often miss many species. So even at the same place, two communities may not be too strongly correlated due to the sampling noise.

sal_marginal <- m1$marginals.fixed$salinity

# Convert to a data frame for plotting the full posterior density
sal_df <- as.data.frame(inla.smarginal(sal_marginal))

ggplot(sal_df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#2166ac") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  # 95% credible interval shading
  geom_ribbon(
    data = subset(sal_df, x >= inla.hpdmarginal(0.95, sal_marginal)[1] &
      x <= inla.hpdmarginal(0.95, sal_marginal)[2]),
    aes(ymin = 0, ymax = y), fill = "#2166ac", alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Posterior distribution — salinity effect",
    x     = "Effect size (log species richness per salinity unit)",
    y     = "Density"
  )









n_samples <- 100
samples <- inla.posterior.sample(n_samples, m1)
beta_int_samples <- sapply(samples, function(s) s$latent["intercept:1", ])
beta_sal_samples <- sapply(samples, function(s) s$latent["salinity:1", ])
sal_seq <- seq(min(data$salinity), max(data$salinity), length.out = 200)

pred_matrix <- outer(rep(1, 200), beta_int_samples) +
  outer(sal_seq, beta_sal_samples)

pred_df <- data.frame(
  salinity = sal_seq,
  fit      = apply(pred_matrix, 1, median),
  lwr      = apply(pred_matrix, 1, quantile, probs = 0.045),
  upr      = apply(pred_matrix, 1, quantile, probs = 0.955)
)

zones <- data.frame(
  xmin  = c(-Inf, 0.5, 5, 18, 30),
  xmax  = c(0.5, 5, 18, 30, Inf),
  label = c("Freshwater", "Oligohaline", "Mesohaline", "Polyhaline", "Euhaline"),
  fill  = c("#a8d5f5", "#d4edda", "#fff3b0", "#f4a96a", "#e07b7b")
)

# Clip zones to your actual data range
x_min_data <- min(data$salinity)
x_max_data <- max(data$salinity)

zones$xmin <- pmax(zones$xmin, x_min_data)
zones$xmax <- pmin(zones$xmax, x_max_data)

# Drop zones outside your data range
zones <- zones[zones$xmin < zones$xmax, ]

ggplot(pred_df, aes(x = salinity)) +
  geom_point(
    data = data, aes(x = salinity, y = log_species_richness),
    alpha = 0.1
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(5, 18, 30),
    linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = zones,
    aes(x = (xmin + xmax) / 2, y = Inf, label = label),
    vjust = 1.5, size = 3.2, colour = "grey30",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = "lightblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Salinity",
    y = "Log Species Richness"
  )

title: How community richness changes along the estuary-sea continuum
section: Modeling alpha, beta and gamma diversity with salinity
text:
Modeling alpha, beta and gamma diversity with salinity
Next, we focus on the different aspects of species diversity

alpha-diversity, that is, the diversity of local communities
beta-diversity, that is, how species composition changes
gamma-diversity, that is, the aggregated diversity

Here, for simplicity we compute beta diversity as the ratio of gamma to alpha diversity.
First, we will focus only on the Garonne estuary, to compare sites that are comparable.

data <- tar_read(fw_with_env) |>
  filter(dist_to_env < 5) |>
  rename(trait = operation_id)

district <- tar_read(fw_with_district) |>
  select(trait = operation_id, year, zone_id, district)

data <- data |>
  left_join(district, by = join_by(trait, year)) |>
  mutate(
    salinity = sali_mean |> as.numeric()
  ) |>
  select(
    trait,
    year,
    survey,
    log_species_richness,
    log_trophic_richness,
    longitude,
    latitude,
    salinity,
    foodweb, #  Now kept to extract species composition.
    district,
    zone_id,
    substrat,
    bathymetry,
    sali_perc_90,
    chl_mean,
    nppv_mean,
    substrat,
    temp_mean,
    temp_cv,
    o2_mean,
    o2_cv,
    wave_mean
  ) |>
  mutate(is_nurse = if_else(survey == "nurse", 1, 0))

data <- data |>
  filter(district == "Ardour-Garonne")

First let’s plot our sampling points and the salinity gradient on a map.

environment_data <- tar_read(environment_data)

coastline <- rnaturalearth::ne_coastline(scale = "large", returnclass = "sf")

e <- c(-0.1, 0.1)
environment_data |>
  group_by(year, x, y) |>
  summarise(salinity = mean(sali_mean), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = salinity)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_sf(data = coastline, inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  geom_point(data, mapping = aes(longitude, latitude), alpha = 0.3) +
  coord_sf(xlim = range(data$longitude) + e, ylim = range(data$latitude) + e) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Salinity [PSU]")








We then compute species composition for each local community to compute the three measure of diversity.

resource_list <- tar_read(resource_list)

get_species <- function(web) {
  sub("_.*", "", colnames(web)) |>
    unique() |>
    setdiff(resource_list)
}

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    species = purrr::map(foodweb, get_species),
    species_richness = purrr::map_dbl(species, length)
  ) |>
  arrange(salinity)

plot_rolling_window <- function(data, window) {
  diversity_df <- purrr::map_dfr(
    seq_len(nrow(data) - window + 1),
    function(i) {
      w <- data[i:(i + window - 1), ]
      tibble(
        salinity = mean(w$salinity),
        gamma = n_distinct(unlist(w$species)),
        alpha = mean(w$species_richness)
      )
    }
  ) |>
    mutate(beta = gamma / alpha) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(alpha, beta, gamma), names_to = "diversity")
  ggplot(diversity_df, aes(salinity, value)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_line() +
    geom_vline(
      xintercept = c(5, 18, 30),
      linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5
    ) +
    facet_wrap("diversity", scales = "free_y") +
    labs(x = "Salinity [PSU]", y = "Community diversity")
}

plot_rolling_window(data, 200)








First, we see that both alpha and gamma diversity increases with salinity, suggesting that communities become richer through the apparition of marine species, and that the brackish diversity is lower.
We observe two peaks in beta diversitt, respectively around 10 and 30 PSU. Those could signals the shift in community due to the transition caused by the presence brackish and marine species respectively.

title: How community richness changes along the estuary-sea continuum
How community richness changes along the estuary-sea continuum
text:
Community composition ordination

Identify the salinity gradient as the main structuring axis
To ordinate communities along the salinity gradient, we first need to build the community matrix which indicate presence and absence of the different species for each site (or here fishing operation).

community_matrix <- data |>
  filter(year > 2000) |>
  select(trait, species, year) |>
  tidyr::unnest(species) |>
  filter_out(species %in% rare_species) |>
  mutate(value = 1) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = species,
    values_fill = 0
  )

Then, we use the package vegan to do an NMDS using the Jaccard distance to measure dissimilarity between communities. Here, we use three dimensions so we have a stress inferior to 0.2, meaning that our ordination is somewhat acceptable.
Next, we want to plot our ordinated communities along the salinity gradient, and visualise which species are driving the change in community composition. Typically, we would expect freshwater and marine species to drive the two ends of the gradient.

scores_df <- as.data.frame(scores(nmds, display = "sites"))

scores_df$salinity <- community_matrix |>
  left_join(data, by = join_by(trait)) |>
  pull(salinity)

scores_df$salinity <- community_matrix |>
  left_join(data, by = join_by(trait)) |>
  pull(salinity)

sp_scores <- as.data.frame(scores(nmds, display = "species"))
sp_scores$species <- rownames(sp_scores)
sp_scores <- sp_scores |>
  mutate(r2 = NMDS1^2 + NMDS2^2) |>
  filter(r2 > quantile(r2, 0.8))

ggplot(scores_df, aes(x = NMDS1, y = NMDS2)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = salinity), size = 2) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  geom_segment(
    data = sp_scores,
    aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = NMDS1, yend = NMDS2),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")),
    colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = sp_scores,
    aes(label = species), size = 3, colour = "grey20",
    nudge_y = 0.02
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = Inf, y = -Inf,
    label = paste("Stress =", round(nmds$stress, 3)),
    hjust = 1.1, vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5, colour = "grey30"
  )








We see that the main structuring axis of the community is salinity as could be expected. Second, we see that marine species (pointing to the right) seems to be the more structuring ones, which are the one we identified previously with our salinity niches. What is less clear is what is the other axis of variation. We could expect the habitat, and so, for example the presence of benthic species to be another structuring axis.
We can plot the our community on the map, coloring with NMDS first axis to see how are structure are communities in space.

scores_df$latitude <- community_matrix |>
  left_join(data, by = join_by(trait)) |>
  pull(latitude)
scores_df$longitude <- community_matrix |>
  left_join(data, by = join_by(trait)) |>
  pull(longitude)

ggplot(scores_df, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = NMDS1)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  geom_sf(data = coastline, inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +
  coord_sf(xlim = range(data$longitude) + e, ylim = range(data$latitude) + e) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)








They are struture along the estuary gradient. In particular, to visualise how salinity structure communities, we can plot the first axis of the NMDS against salinity.

scores_df$log_species_richness <- community_matrix |>
  left_join(data, by = join_by(trait)) |>
  pull(log_species_richness)

ggplot(scores_df, aes(x = salinity, y = NMDS1)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = log_species_richness), size = 2) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = "Salinity", colour = "Log Species\nRichness")








We see a positive association. As suggested by the relative high stress of the NMDS (~0.18), the community are difficult to ordinate. This may be due to to the noise related to the sampling process, sometimes we do not fish all species that are there. It may also be due to the fact that we aggregate points over the year and so we have differencies from one year to another.


Identify structuring variables beyond salinity
We want to do a more general analysis to find which environmental variables structure our communities.

env <- data |>
  select(
    trait, salinity, bathymetry, o2_mean, chl_mean, nppv_mean,
    temp_mean, year
  ) |>
  right_join(community_matrix |> select(trait, year), by = join_by(trait, year)) |>
  select(-c(trait, year))

fit <- envfit(nmds, env)

fit_df <- as.data.frame(scores(fit, display = "vectors"))
fit_df$variable <- rownames(fit_df)
fit_df$r2 <- fit$vectors$r
fit_df$p <- fit$vectors$pvals
fit_df <- fit_df |> filter(p <= 0.05)

ggplot(scores_df, aes(x = NMDS1, y = NMDS2)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = log_species_richness), size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  geom_segment(
    data = fit_df,
    aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = NMDS1, yend = NMDS2),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")),
    colour = "black", linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = fit_df,
    aes(
      x = NMDS1 * 1.15, y = NMDS2 * 1.15,
      label = paste0(variable, "\nR²=", round(r2, 2))
    ),
    size = 3, fill = "white", label.size = 0.2
  ) +
  labs(colour = "Log Species Richness")








We recover that most of the structure is driven by the salinity gradient and the correlated variable.

We can have a look at the evolution of average temperature with years.

env |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(annual_temperature = mean(temp_mean), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = annual_temperature)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean annual temperature")








However, this is not very informative because we do not account for the spatialization of the data. A better way, to investigate the data is to plot yearly map of the different environmental variables. For example, below we plot the distribution of mean oxygen level, chorophyl concentration, and temperature.

library(tidyr)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(rnaturalearthhires)

coastline <- ne_coastline(scale = "large", returnclass = "sf")

var_list <- c("o2_mean", "nppv_mean", "temp_mean")
year_list <- c(2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023)

env_long <- env |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      chl_mean, nppv_mean, o2_mean, o2_cv,
      o2_perc_25, temp_mean, temp_cv, temp_perc_90, sali_mean
    ),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  filter(year %in% year_list & variable %in% var_list) |>
  mutate(value_scaled = scale(value)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(env_long, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = value_scaled)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_sf(data = coastline, inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_grid(variable ~ year) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  coord_sf(xlim = range(env$x), ylim = range(env$y))








We can also plot the salinity for a given year, say 2023. We use a log scale, as salinity changes a lot in the estuary.

env |>
  mutate(log_salinity = log10(sali_mean)) |>
  filter(year == 2023) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = log_salinity)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_sf(data = coastline, inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  coord_sf(xlim = range(env$x), ylim = range(env$y)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)









env |>
  mutate(chlorophyll = chl_mean) |>
  filter(year == 2023) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = chlorophyll)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_sf(data = coastline, inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  coord_sf(xlim = range(env$x), ylim = range(env$y)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)








We see that different environmental variables seem correlated. We can have a look at them more exhaustively with pairwise scatterplot.

cols <- c(
  "chl_mean", "nppv_mean", "o2_mean", "temp_mean", "sali_mean",
  "bathymetry"
)
year_vals <- c(2000, 2010, 2020)
GGally::ggpairs(
  env |> mutate(year = as.factor(year)) |> filter(year %in% year_vals),
  columns = cols,
  aes(colour = year, alpha = 0.1)
)








First, we see that we have some strong correlations between variables, such as, between oxygen and temperature. Interestingly, there are also changes between the correlation between the variables. In particular, we see that in the recent years, there is now a very strong correlation between chlorophyll and net primary productivity. This seems to be due to an explosion in primary productivity values in recent years. This is probably due to a change in the way the productivity is computed, but let’s further investigate.

year_list <- c(2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023)

ggplot(
  env |> filter(year %in% year_list),
  aes(x = x, y = y, fill = nppv_mean)
) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_sf(data = coastline, inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~year) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-1.5, -0.5), ylim = c(44.8, 45.8))








We see indeed an explosion of the net primary productivity in the Gironde and Loire estuaries.
For comparison let’s plot cholorophyll values.

ggplot(
  env |> filter(year %in% year_list),
  aes(x = x, y = y, fill = chl_mean)
) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_sf(data = coastline, inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~year) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-1.5, -0.5), ylim = c(44.8, 45.8))

text:
Matching food web and environmental data
We match food webs with the closest environmental data available. We also record the distance between the foodweb and the environmental data, so we can later filter out food webs for which we don’t environmental data available (e.g. if the distance is greater than 20 km).

fw_with_env <- tar_read(fw_with_env)

Next, we want to check that the distance to environmental data is consistent with our expectation, that is, the distance is low for the atlantic coast, and increases as we go further into the Manche.

ggplot(fw_with_env, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = dist_to_env)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_sf(data = coastline, inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +

  coord_sf(
    xlim = range(fw_with_env$longitude),
    ylim = range(fw_with_env$latitude)
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)









dist_max <- 20

Let’s say, that we want to keep only food webs for which with have environmental variables closer than 20 km, and map them.

ggplot(
  fw_with_env |> filter(dist_to_env < dist_max),
  aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = dist_to_env)
) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +

  coord_sf(

    ylim = range(fw_with_env$latitude)

  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)

title: Infer missing fish sizes
text:
Summary
In this notebook, we

we infer missing fish sizes for sea campagnes assuming a normal distribution
validate our inference using cross-validation



0. Setup

library(renv)
renv::load()
renv::status() # Check the project state.

library(targets)
library(here)
tar_config_set(
  store = here::here("_targets")
)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggVennDiagram)
set_theme(theme_minimal())
library(riversea)



1. Illustrate the inference with synthetic data
The idea of the inference is quite simple. We observe a given distribution of values, representing fish sizes. We assume that the underlying distribution is a normal distribution. This choice can be seen as a choice toward simplicity. We say that we only know about the mean and the variance of the distribution, and in this case the most probable distribution is a normal distribution.
To begin with, we illustrate the procedure on synthetic data. So let’s simulate values from a normal distribution.

n <- 1000 # Sample size.
obs <- rnorm(n)
n_missing <- 100
obs_missing <- data.frame(true = rnorm(n_missing))

infer_missing_sizes <- function(obs, n_missing) {
  mu <- mean(obs)
  sigma <- sd(obs)
  rnorm(n_missing, mu, sigma)
}

obs_missing$pred <- infer_missing_sizes(obs, n_missing)

ggplot(obs_missing, aes(x = true, y = pred)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1)








We see that this method is quite bad at predicting fish size at the individual level. But what really matters is whether the infered distribution of missing sizes corresponds to the true one.

obs_missing_long <- obs_missing |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(true, pred),
    names_to = "type",
    values_to = "value"
  )

ggplot(obs_missing_long, aes(x = value, fill = type)) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.5, position = "identity")








We see that here it works quite well, because the sample size is large, and we are sampling missing values from a normal distribution, which won’t be the case for real data.


2. Apply the methods to campagne data

title: Validate the diet table
text:
Code
library(renv)
renv::load()
renv::status() # Check the project state.
library(targets)
library(here)
tar_config_set(
  store = here::here("_targets")
)
library(riversea)
We now source the diet table for estuarine and coastal fish from a literature-validated table (data/diet/marine_diet_validated.csv) instead of the fishbase scrape.
We first go over sanity checks to ensure that the diet table is consistent, and the resulting food webs as well.

title: Validate the diet table
text:
Sanity checks

Species coverage
We compare the species observed often enough in the sea surveys to the species covered by the diet table. A species is considered non-rare if it was caught strictly more than params$occurence_min times. The table below lists commonly observed species missing from the diet table; empty means no coverage gap.

params <- tar_read(params)
diet <- tar_read(diet)
catch <- tar_read(sea_data_tidy)$catch

check_diet_species_coverage(diet, catch, params$occurence_min)

character(0)




Size coverage per species
For each species, the diet table should define a diet over contiguous stages covering the whole size range, from 0 to unbounded, otherwise foodwebbuilder::build_metaweb() errors out on a missing diet interval. We look for three failure modes: gaps between consecutive stages, a first stage that does not start at 0, and a last stage that does not reach an unbounded size.

check_diet_size_coverage(diet)

# A tibble: 0 × 3
# ℹ 3 variables: species <chr>, issue <chr>, detail <chr>




Metaweb consistency
We also check the metaweb built from this diet table: every non-resource (fish) trophic species should have at least one prey item, and no trophic species should be fully disconnected (neither predator nor prey of anything).

web_list <- tar_read(web_list)
resource_list <- tar_read(resource_list)

check_metaweb_consistency(web_list$metaweb, resource_list)

# A tibble: 0 × 2
# ℹ 2 variables: species <chr>, issue <chr>


If the three tables above are all empty, the diet table and the metaweb built from it pass every automated check.
