  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = inland,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0,
    names_prefix = "inland_"
  ) |>
  rename(
    inland = inland_TRUE,
    "sea-side" = inland_FALSE,
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

Catchment attribution
Next, we want to attribute a catchment to the sea operations. We proceed as follows: if the operation is inland, we use the district of the basin it falls in; if the operation is sea-side, we use the district of the closest coastal water body. Here, the question is to define a threshold beyond which we consider that a coastal water body cannot be reliably attributed to an operation. To help us, let’s plot, in the Gironde estuary, the operations farthest from the closest water body.


Code
operation_year_filtered <- tar_read(operation_year_filtered)

outside_sea <- operation_year_filtered |>
  filter(survey != "river") |>
  sf::st_as_sf(
    coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE
  ) |>
  sf::st_join(basin["district"], join = sf::st_within) |>
  filter(is.na(district)) |>
  select(-district)

nearest_idx <- sf::st_nearest_feature(outside_sea, coastal_water)
outside_sea <- outside_sea |>
  mutate(dist_km = as.numeric(sf::st_distance(
    outside_sea, coastal_water[nearest_idx, ],
    by_element = TRUE
  )) / 1000)

thresholds <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20)
tibble::tibble(threshold_km = thresholds) |>
  mutate(
    pct_matched = round(
      100 * purrr::map_dbl(threshold_km, \(t) mean(outside_sea$dist_km <= t)),
      1
    ),
    n_unmatched = purrr::map_int(
      threshold_km, \(t) sum(outside_sea$dist_km > t)
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

Inland operations: snapping quality
Sea operations split in two: inland and sea-side. Inland operations are snapped to the river network and their distance to the river mouth is computed as for river operations. Sea-side operations are not on the river network, and Euclidean distance cannot be used directly, because a straight line can cut across land. For this reason, we compute distance along a mesh that excludes land.
First, we check that inland operations are snapped correctly to the river network by looking at their snapping distance.


Code
threshold_sea <- 2100
sea_stations_selected <- tar_read(inland_operations_snapped) |>
  filter(survey != "river")

ggplot(sea_stations_selected, aes(x = snap_dist_m)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#a9c9e0", color = "white", bins = 40) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = threshold_sea) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = threshold_sea, y = Inf, label = paste0(threshold_sea, "m"),
    hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    trans = "log10", labels = scales::label_number(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Snapping distance (m)", y = "Number of operations")









Because sea survey operations sit in wide estuaries, we expect greater snapping distances than for operations in thin river branches. For this reason, we have raised the threshold to 2100. This value was selected through visual investigation of the Gironde and Seine estuaries, such that all their operations are recovered. This visual investigation allowed us to identify an operation, 61837633, which turned out to be miscoded inland right at the coast and is now classified sea-side directly in classify_operation_location().


Sea-side operations: mesh
We build a water-only mesh (see build_sea_mesh()), which we convert into a graph and run the Dijkstra algorithm to compute the distance between the operation and the closest river mouth (per catchment).
Here is the mesh we built. We zoomed in on two coastal areas to show how it follows the land.

The mesh covers water only; land, including islands, is left untriangulated, as desired.
Next, we show, using an example from l’île de Ré, how the mesh-based distance is computed depending on whether a straight line between the operation and the river mouth crosses land.


Code
sea_dist <- tar_read(sea_offshore_distance_to_mouth)
mouth_kept <- river_mouth_district |>
  filter(matched, district %in% district_kept) |>
  st_as_sf() |>
  st_transform(4326)
mouth_kept$node_id <- snap_to_sea_graph(mouth_kept, sea_graph)$node_id

sea_dist_sf <- sea_dist |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)
crossing_len <- straight_line_land_crossing(
  sea_dist_sf, mouth_kept, sea_mesh$land, district_kept
)
sea_dist_checked <- sea_dist |> left_join(crossing_len, by = "operation_id")

pick_pair <- function(xlim, ylim) {
  in_zoom <- sea_dist_checked |>
    filter(
      longitude >= xlim[1], longitude <= xlim[2],
      latitude >= ylim[1], latitude <= ylim[2]
    )
  crossing <- in_zoom |>
    filter(crossing_len_m > 100) |>
    arrange(desc(crossing_len_m)) |>
    slice(1)
  clean <- in_zoom |> filter(crossing_len_m == 0) |> slice(1)
  list(crossing = crossing, clean = clean)
}

pair_islands <- pick_pair(zoom_islands$xlim, zoom_islands$ylim)

plot_pair <- function(op_row, label) {
  path <- sea_mouth_path(op_row, mouth_kept, sea_graph)
  plot_sea_path_checkpoint(op_row, path, mesh_edges, sea_mesh$land, label)
}

p1 <- plot_pair(
  pair_islands$crossing, "Ile de Re - crosses land"
)
p2 <- plot_pair(
  pair_islands$clean, "Ile de Re - doesn't cross land"
)

p1 + p2









Where the straight line would cut across land, the mesh path detours around it and comes out longer; where it wouldn’t, the mesh path stays close to the straight-line distance.
